claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized as a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the BCC phase at high temperature.
Strong Al-Ni interactions govern local atomic ordering in this alloy.
The relevant Al-Ni interactions are repulsive or ordering interactions.
Al-Ni pairwise interactions create a thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
Specific chemical interactions raise the thermodynamic instability of competing phases.
The alloy has a high nucleation barrier that kinetically suppresses transformation during rapid cooling.
Local ordering promotes compositional inhomogeneity and secondary-phase nucleation when sufficient diffusion occurs.
Slow cooling permits atomic rearrangement into lower-energy multiphase configurations.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and nucleation, kinetically trapping the high-temperature BCC structure.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will retain a largely homogeneous BCC microstructure.
Slowly cooled Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will develop secondary phases such as ordered precipitates.
Temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution, including low-temperature intermetallic formation, occurs in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily when diffusion kinetics control the phase response and for compositions near Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Intermediate cooling rates or impurity-driven nucleation may cause deviations from the predicted trend.
A controlled rapid-quench versus slow-furnace-cooling comparison can test the proposed kinetic effect while holding composition, geometry, atmosphere, and prior heat treatment constant.
Retention of BCC without secondary-phase formation in both the rapidly quenched and slowly cooled samples would falsify the stated hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the interactions raise the instability of competing phases, which would favor retention of BCC, whereas the mechanism says those same interactions create the thermodynamic drive for phase separation into competing phases.

The Al-Ni interaction is ambiguously characterized as either repulsive or ordering: repulsion is used to motivate phase separation, while local ordering is used to motivate ordered precipitates, without specifying which interaction applies or reconciling these distinct responses.
